name: Navajo National Monument
author: author-D-2026-10-18
summary:
In sheltered alcoves of the Tsegi Canyon system, cut deep into the Navajo sandstone of the Shonto Plateau and surrounded by the lands of the Navajo Nation, stand the three primary cliff villages Ancestral Puebloan people built in the final, Tsegi phase of the Pueblo III period, about AD 1250 to 1300: Betatakin, Keet Seel and Inscription House. The Foundation Document counts them among the largest and most intact precontact structures in the Southwest. [1] Betatakin was lived in only a short time between 1250 and 1300. Keet Seel was older; some people settled there by 950, building surged in 1272, and its population may have approached 150. About 1300 its last residents left, sealing the doorways of rooms that held jars of corn. The brochure lists drought, erosion, social pressures and religious dictates among the possible reasons, and says the contemporary Pueblo people emerged from the migrations that followed. [1]

President William H. Taft proclaimed the monument on March 20, 1909, setting aside 160 square miles before, as historian Hal Rothman notes, anyone from the government had seen the ruins; in 1912 it was cut to three tracts totaling 360 acres. [1] [1] It had only a volunteer custodian until 1938, and paved roads did not reach the visitor center until 1965. Under a 1962 agreement the Navajo Nation let the Park Service use land on the canyon rim for its headquarters, and Rothman describes the park and its Shonto-region neighbors as interdependent to a degree unequaled in the park system. [1] Inscription House has been closed to visitors since 1968 to protect it; about 66,000 people a year visited when the 2017 Foundation Document was written. [1]

indigenous.html:
The Hopi call the builders Hisatsinom, their ancestors, and the villages Talastima (Betatakin), Kawestima (Keet Seel) and Tsu’ovi (Inscription House), believed to be stops on migration paths of at least eight clans; Hopi elders still make pilgrimages. [1] [1] To the Zuni, the Tsegi region is the “northern canyons,” where several clans originated. San Juan Southern Paiute people lived in Tsegi Canyon and near Inscription House; the Foundation Document dates their Shonto Plateau occupation from the late 1600s through the 1800s. [1] [1]

The villages’ best-known names are Diné: Betatakin, “ledge house,” and Keet Seel, from a word for “broken pottery scattered around.” The Foundation Document says the Navajo were thought to have entered the region in the 17th century, or centuries earlier by some traditional accounts; the brochure dates their arrival nearby to the 1800s; Rothman, that Navajos settled around Navajo Mountain to avoid confinement at the Bosque Redondo in the 1860s. Taft’s 1909 proclamation called them “extraordinary ruins of an unknown people.” [1] [1] [1]

labor_ccc.html:
Rothman’s 1991 history traces the monument’s changing Navajo labor force. New Deal money paid its first seasonal laborers, among them Bob Black, who started in 1935 and stayed 31 years. In 1947, when wage discrimination was the rule in the U.S., the Park Service paid its Navajo laborers the same $1.15 an hour as non-Indian workers. Seth Bigman, a World War II veteran, became the first Navajo seasonal ranger in 1948, and in 1958 a tribal council member threatened to shut down a stabilization project at Inscription House because it employed no Navajos. [1]

By the mid-1960s the maintenance staff was all Navajo except its supervisor. In 1982, when five of the nine permanent employees were Navajo, all five held lower grades than their Anglo and Hispano colleagues. John Laughter became the first Navajo permanent supervisor in the mid-1980s; Clarence N. Gorman, a Navajo, became superintendent in 1986. By 1990 eight of eleven employees were Navajo. [1]

facts.claim: Tsegi Canyon, primary drainage of the eastern Shonto Plateau, cut into Navajo sandstone; pueblo complexes in sheltered alcoves of the Tsegi Canyon system; Inscription House in Nitsin Canyon; monument surrounded by Navajo Nation lands

Betatakin, Keet Seel and Inscription House built by Ancestral Puebloans in the Tsegi phase of Pueblo III (approx. AD 1250–1300); considered among the largest and most intact precontact structures in the southwestern U.S.
Betatakin inhabited only a short time between 1250 and 1300
Keet Seel: some people settled by 950; building surged 1272; population may have approached 150; about 1300 last residents departed, sealing doorways of rooms containing pottery jars of corn
Withdrawal possibly caused by drought, erosion, social pressures, religious dictates or other influences; from the migrations emerged the contemporary Pueblo people
Taft proclamation March 20, 1909 under the Antiquities Act; initially 160 square miles; March 14, 1912 reduced to three tracts totaling 360 acres (Betatakin 160, Keet Seel 160, Inscription House 40)
Establishment: Navajo National Monument March 20, 1909
"No one from the government had yet seen the ruins" when the original proclamation was issued
Only a volunteer custodian from 1909 until 1938; paved roads to the Visitor Center completed 1965; Memorandum of Agreement May 1962
MOA: use of Navajo land on the rim of Betatakin Canyon in exchange for privileges (craft sales area)
Interdependence unequaled elsewhere in the national park system
Inscription House closed to visitors since 1968; about 66,000 visitors per year

Hisatsinom, ancestors of the Hopi, built the villages; villages believed to have been stops along sacred migration paths of at least eight Hopi clans; elders annually visit; Hopi elders still make pilgrimages
Hopi names Talastima (Betatakin), Kawestima (Keet Seel), Tsu'ovi (Inscription House); Hopi clan members continue to visit sites to make offerings
Zuni: Tsegi Canyon region known as the "northern canyons," from which several clans originated

San Juan Southern Paiute lived in Tsegi Canyon and near Inscription House (brochure also says "for many hundreds of years" — not used, as the FD dates their Shonto Plateau occupation from the late 1600s)

The two largest villages best known by names given by the Navajo people who arrived in the vicinity during the 1800s; Betatakin means "ledge house" in Navajo; Keet Seel from an altered Navajo word meaning "broken pottery scattered around"
Navajo thought to have entered the region in the 17th century, if not several hundreds of years earlier according to some traditional accounts

Navajos had begun to settle in the area to avoid the forced confinement at the Bosque Redondo near Fort Sumner in the 1860s; fleeing the American military, they found the area around Navajo Mountain far enough from the cavalry
1909 proclamation reserved "extraordinary ruins of an unknown people"
New Deal provided money for the first seasonal laborers, among them Bob Black, who began in 1935 and remained 31 years
1947: NPS paid Navajo laborers the same rate as non-Indian workers ($1.15/hour) when wage discrimination was the rule in the U.S.
1948 Seth Bigman, WWII veteran, first Navajo seasonal ranger
1958 Tribal Council member Paul Begay threatened to close a stabilization project at Inscription House because it employed no Navajos
Mid-1960s maintenance staff exclusively Navajo except the supervisor; mid-1980s John Laughter first Navajo in a permanent supervisory capacity
1982: five of nine permanent employees Navajo; all Anglos and the Hispano had higher GS ranks than the five Navajos
Clarence N. Gorman, a Navajo who once worked as a seasonal ranger, appointed superintendent 1986
By 1990 eleven full- and part-time employees, eight Navajo including the superintendent and maintenance head
(FD) Beginning in the late 1600s and continuing through the 1800s, the San Juan Southern Paiute occupied areas on the Shonto Plateau
